section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from early to mid-1940 concerning political developments and foreign policy in Japan. It includes analyses of Japanese military psychology and domestic fascism, the resignation of Prime Minister Nobuyuki Abe and the formation of Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai's cabinet, and mounting pressure from the Japanese Army for an authoritarian internal political structure and a pro-Axis foreign policy. The section concludes with the forced resignation of the Yonai Cabinet in July 1940, the return to power of Prince Fumimaro Konoe, and international reactions from Washington, Moscow, Berlin, and Batavia.

subfiles.about: A military study analyzing the psychological and cultural factors governing Japanese soldier behavior and proposing American defensive tactics.
subfiles.summary: This excerpt analyzes the fanatical fighting psychology of the Japanese soldier, rooted in Shintoism, emperor-worship, and a conviction of divine mission. It highlights characteristics such as rigid adherence to initial battle plans, contempt for defense or retirement, and readiness for suicidal sacrifice, as exemplified by the 'three human bombs' at Shanghai. The author cautions against young officers and students driven by extremist nationalism, while noting underlying weaknesses in Japanese military technology, pilot training, and economic stability. Finally, it recommends that American commanders counter Japanese offensive fanaticism with layered defensive firepower—automatic weapons, artillery, and mechanized forces—rather than meeting infantry charges bayonet-to-bayonet.
subfiles.title: The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier

subfiles.about: Acknowledging receipt of an article entitled 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier' prepared by Captain Bonner F. Fellers.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Mr. Bergman for Captain Bonner Fellers's article 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier', read with interest.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Mr. Bergman regarding 'The Psychology of the Japanese Soldier'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a telegram from Tokyo reporting on Admiral Nomura's views on Pacific questions and Diet proceedings.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Telegram No. 80 (February 3, 1940, 793.94/15647): changing Japanese attitudes on Far Eastern and Pacific questions, the Diet, and Nomura's view that some US actions are inadvisable.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Changing Japanese Attitude toward General Far Eastern and Pacific Questions

subfiles.about: Transmitting a confidential memorandum by Hallett Abend on statements made by K. Obata of the Japanese Foreign Office regarding Army extremism, Wang Ching-wei, and the Tientsin blockade.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General C. E. Gauss transmits a confidential memorandum by New York Times correspondent Hallett Abend recounting his interviews in Shanghai with K. Obata of the American Affairs Section of the Gaimusho. Obata deplored the unchecked dominance of radical Army elements and the inability of Foreign Office moderates to check them or avert potential violent uprisings. Obata agreed with Abend that the Japanese government had mishandled the establishment of Wang Ching-wei's puppet regime, suggesting the project be dropped to preserve the chance of restoring relations with the United States, and proposed Abend secretly visit Tokyo to advise Japanese leaders. Regarding the Tientsin blockade, Obata claimed General Homma was privately pro-British but powerless against unruly younger subordinate officers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 841 from Shanghai: Statements Made by Mr. K. Obata to Mr. Hallett Abend

subfiles.about: Analyzing the background of General Abe's resignation and the appointment of Admiral Yonai as Prime Minister.
subfiles.summary: Coville summarizes Despatch No. 4486: Abe fell through inexperience and procrastination; Hata said the Army could no longer support him, and the Emperor commanded cooperation. Yonai became compromise premier.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Resignation of the Abe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting in detail on the political crisis surrounding the fall of the Abe Cabinet and the formation, personnel, and policies of the Yonai Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides a comprehensive account of the collapse of Prime Minister General Nobuyuki Abe's cabinet and the formation of a successor administration under Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai. The Abe Cabinet collapsed after less than five months due to administrative missteps, disputes over a proposed Trade Ministry, deteriorating economic conditions marked by inflation and commodity maldistribution, and widespread Diet revolt. When War Minister Hata withdrew Army backing, imperial advisers led by Prince Konoe and Kurahei Yuasa maneuvered the Army into a corner by urging it to assume direct prime ministerial responsibility, which it refused, resulting in an imperial admonition to cooperate with whatever cabinet was formed. Yonai assembled a diverse transitional cabinet of experienced bureaucrats, party figures, and military officers aimed at restoring stability and testing the national temper while maintaining existing continental and non-involvement policies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4486 from Tokyo: Resignation of the Abe Cabinet -- Selection of Admiral Yonai as Prime Minister and the Composition and Policies of His Cabinet

subfiles.about: Clarifying Ambassador Grew's remarks to Sir Stafford Cripps concerning the prospects of a military dictatorship in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew says Cripps misquoted him to Craigie as predicting dictatorship; Grew sees Japan evolving more liberal, with military control only temporary in a crisis such as food riots.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 182 from Tokyo: Conversation with Sir Stafford Cripps Regarding Japanese Politics

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a review of Japan's foreign relations and domestic situation during the year 1939.
subfiles.summary: Indexes Despatch No. 4574 (March 11, 1940, 794.00/171): Grew's review of Japan's relations with the powers and domestic situation in 1939.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Japan's Relations with Principal Powers and Internal Situation during 1939

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing information from Miss Midkiff of the Y.W.C.A. on Japanese policies and restrictions during the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Indexes a May 8, 1940 YWCA letter (793.94/15867) transmitting Miss Midkiff's information on Japanese policies, wartime restrictions and reactions.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Sino-Japanese Conflict Information from Miss Midkiff

subfiles.about: Relaying a report from the American Consulate in Taihoku regarding the arrest of consular employee Matsuo on charges of violating military secrets laws.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays consul Warner at Taihoku: consular employee Matsuo arrested under military secrets laws; charges unstated and visits refused. Warner links it to his consulate duties.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 359 from Tokyo: Arrest of Consular Employee Matsuo at Taihoku

subfiles.about: Summarizing an Osaka consular report on Tei-ichi Muto and his fascist, pro-Axis, and anti-Semitic organization 'Sai-sei'.
subfiles.summary: Coville summarizes Osaka Consul Allison's report on Tei-ichi Muto's fascist 'Sai-sei' organization: nationalistic Shinto, totalitarian government, German alliance, anti-Jewish activity, and seizure of the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum: Activities of Mr. Tei-ichi Muto and the Organization 'Sai-sei'

subfiles.about: Reporting on the fascist, pro-Axis, and anti-Semitic activities of journalist Tei-ichi Muto and his 'Sai-sei' movement centered in western Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Consul John M. Allison reports on the political and ideological movement led by Tei-ichi Muto, former Osaka Asahi columnist and assistant editor of the Osaka Jiji Shimpo. Muto heads 'Sai-sei' (Saisei Itchi, or Unity of Religion and Government), an organization that blends Shinto emperor-worship with Nazi-style totalitarianism, using the title 'shu-mei' for its leader. The movement attacks democratic political parties, Christian missionaries, the Salvation Army, and Jews, while advocating a Rome-Berlin-Tokyo axis and Japanese expansion into the resource-rich South Seas to counter American economic leverage. Allison notes that Muto is backed financially by industrialist Koichiro Ishihara and enjoys close ties with sympathetic Army officers and youth associations in the Kansai region.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Osaka: Activities of Mr. Tei-ichi Muto and the Organization 'Sai-sei'

subfiles.about: Reporting the establishment of regular Four-Minister conferences to formulate Japanese high national policy in response to European developments.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports plans for twice-weekly Four-Minister 'inner cabinet' conferences on China and international policy; the press ties the European war to the Far East.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 386 from Tokyo: Establishment of Four-Minister Inner Cabinet

subfiles.about: Assessing the policy implications of the newly established Four-Minister conference in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Grew appraises the Four-Minister council: expect no immediate policy departures, since fundamental changes need wider consultation with senior statesmen.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 387 from Tokyo: Appraisal of the Four-Minister Council

subfiles.about: Reporting British intelligence that the German Embassy is actively fostering a single-party fascist system in Japan and keeping US-Japan relations strained.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays Craigie: a German DNB agent said Germany is promoting a Japanese single-party system, keeping US-Japan relations strained, and plans to turn on Russia. Craigie protested.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 423 from Tokyo: German Efforts to Promote a Single Party System in Japan

subfiles.about: Reporting British views on German diplomatic intrigue in Tokyo and rumors of unofficial Soviet-Japanese conversations in Moscow.
subfiles.summary: Thurston reports the British Chargé will not act on Tokyo telegram 423 before Cripps arrives, and Thurston declines without instructions. Moscow rumors of Japanese-Soviet contacts on China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 655 from Moscow: British Views on German Activities and Soviet-Japanese Contacts

subfiles.about: Approving Chargé Thurston's decision to refrain from communicating German-Japanese intelligence to the Soviet Government.
subfiles.summary: Hull approves Thurston's refusal to approach the Soviet Government about German Embassy activities in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 325 to Moscow: Approval of Inaction on German Intelligence

subfiles.about: Reporting press rumors that Prince Konoe will resign as President of the Privy Council and be succeeded by Baron Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the press predicts Konoe will resign as Privy Council president, with Hiranuma replacing him.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 486 from Tokyo: Rumored Resignation of Prince Konoe from Privy Council

subfiles.about: Reporting Prince Konoe's formal resignation from the Privy Council amid speculation he will form a new cabinet or lead a single-party movement.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoe resigned as Privy Council president, perhaps to form a cabinet or lead the Single Party Movement; Hara succeeds, with no special significance.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 489 from Tokyo: Resignation of Prince Konoe and Political Speculation

subfiles.about: Analyzing political maneuvers and speculation surrounding Prince Konoe's resignation and pressure on him to lead a new national structure.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports speculation on Konoe's moves: he'll help build a national structure but not for partisan intrigue, and likely will form a government by mid-July on his own terms.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 494 from Tokyo: Speculation on Prince Konoe's Political Moves

subfiles.about: Reporting Japanese press accounts of a Cabinet decision defining an independent foreign policy and an East Asian sphere.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports press accounts of a Cabinet-approved policy: non-involvement in the European war, settling the China incident, East Asian 'Monroe Doctrine', no break with the US and Britain nor subservience to the Axis.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 500 from Tokyo: Cabinet Decision on Japan's High Diplomatic Policy

subfiles.about: Outlining press summaries of an impending foreign policy declaration by Foreign Minister Arita calling for the redistribution of territories and resources.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Arita expected to issue a foreign policy statement drafted by Suma, sharing the Axis aim of redistributing territories and excluding third-power interference. Nichi Nichi cites the Monroe Doctrine.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 506 from Tokyo: Impending Declaration of Foreign Policy by Foreign Minister

subfiles.about: Reporting confidential information that Prime Minister Yonai disavowed press accounts of an aggressive foreign policy declaration as an unauthorized leak by pro-Axis elements.
subfiles.summary: Grew relays that Yonai disavowed the press-published aggressive foreign policy statement, which a pro-Axis Foreign Office group leaked to force the Cabinet's hand.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Tokyo (Continuing 506): Prime Minister Yonai Disavows Press Reports of Foreign Policy Statement

subfiles.about: Informing the Tokyo Embassy of Secretary Hull's press conference remarks regarding Admiral Nomura's visit to Davao, T.V. Soong, and the May export control bill.
subfiles.summary: Hull says he knew only press reports of Nomura's Davao visit; the transcript covers a T. V. Soong call and the May Bill export embargo authority, to be run by an interdepartmental coordinator.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 239 to Tokyo with Excerpt from Secretary Hull's Press Conference

subfiles.about: Summarizing Prince Konoe's press interview outlining his concepts for a permanent new national political structure and civil-military coordination.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a summary and Department paraphrase of a press interview given by Prince Fumimaro Konoe on July 7 regarding the proposed 'new political structure'. Konoe stated that the organization must be permanent rather than an expedient for the China incident, insisted the Diet and existing parties would not be eliminated, and rejected forming a totalitarian single party modeled on Germany or Italy. Instead, he envisioned mobilizing national political power under the Cabinet, possibly through an economic congress of occupational representatives, while strictly preserving the Imperial Constitution. Grew assesses that Konoe's moderate concepts will likely result in an innocuous compromise that disappoints extremist factions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 548 from Tokyo: Prince Konoe's Views on the Proposed New Political Structure (with Paraphrase)

subfiles.about: Urgent report from Tokyo stating that the Yonai Cabinet will resign tonight.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports a reliable contact says Yonai's entire Cabinet will resign tonight, July 16, 1940.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 584 from Tokyo: Impending Resignation of the Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Confirming the formal resignation of the entire Yonai Cabinet on July 16, 1940.
subfiles.summary: Grew confirms the entire Yonai Cabinet resigned at 5:30 p.m. on July 16, 1940.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 585 from Tokyo: Resignation of the Entire Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Detailing the circumstances and press reactions surrounding the fall of the Yonai Cabinet due to War Minister Hata's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports press agreement that the Yonai Cabinet fell over an Army-Yonai rift; Hata resigned after Yonai rejected his demands. Konoe expected to form the next cabinet, with Matsuoka or Shiratori for Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 590 from Tokyo: Background and Press Reactions to the Fall of the Yonai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting intense anxiety among Netherlands East Indies authorities in Batavia following the fall of the Yonai Cabinet and fears of Japanese expansion.
subfiles.summary: Consul General Dickover reports Netherlands Indies officials fear Japan, with German backing, will seize European territories and hope the American fleet will protect them.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Batavia: Netherlands Indies Apprehensions over Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Reporting that Prince Fumimaro Konoe was commanded by the Emperor to form a new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the Emperor commanded Prince Konoe to form a new Cabinet on July 17, 1940.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 591 from Tokyo: Prince Konoe Commanded to Form New Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting progress on the formation of the new Konoe Cabinet and candidates for Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Konoe choosing a cabinet, with Matsuoka, Shiratori and Togo rumored for Foreign Minister. A full assessment will follow.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 592 from Tokyo: Formation of the Second Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reporting German semi-official commentary viewing the Japanese cabinet change as an Army move to free Japan from Western tutelage.
subfiles.summary: Kirk reports the German press largely silent on Japan's cabinet change; a semi-official commentary blames Army dissatisfaction with Yonai's failure to break from Western tutelage.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 3016 from Berlin: German Reaction to the Japanese Cabinet Change

subfiles.about: Reporting the agenda of the four-minister Supreme National Defense Conference, including axis strengthening and civil-military reorganization.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports the agenda of the Supreme National Defense Conference: reexamining non-involvement, strengthening the Axis, a defense state, China, and unifying military command with civil administration.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 603 from Tokyo: Agenda of Supreme National Defense Conference
